items.title: Kristen Korb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000
items.q: But man every once in a while I will hear a Sarah Vaughan lick come out of her, it’s just you know, some of those half step [scats] kinds of things. I just go — that was a Sarah Vaughan thing.

ctx.x: That was such a big part of that era of the music is people having their own identifiable sound.

And I think today’s guys, I mean everybody’s got their own sound. Even though we’ve got a lot of kind of clone people. But I think if you listen to them long enough I think at this point we’ve listened to those guys so long now that it seems more obvious to us. Where with a lot of these younger guys we still haven’t listened to them enough. Because I’m getting to the point now where I can hear Russell in about three notes. But I’ve been doing a lot of listening. I want to play with him so I’m listening to his…

being very eclectic with her music, you know, borrowing from pop, borrowing from jazz. She’s doing a little bit of world music kinds of things. Very creative. But man every once in a while I will hear a Sarah Vaughan lick come out of her, it’s just you know, some of those half step [scats] kinds of things. I just go — that was a Sarah Vaughan thing. But she’s still Dianne. When Ray plays “Swing Until The Girls Come Home,” that’s Oscar Pettiford, but it’s still Ray.
